presenceLabel: Yuchi towns in the Southeast (none documented in Kentucky)
presenceNote: First documented: ‘Uchi’ and ‘Huchi’ in the Pardo expedition of 1567. Drawn: the eastern Tennessee valley to 1714, the Savannah River c.1722–1751 and the Chattahoochee River 1715–1836. The Kentucky story rests on one hedged line in Swanton (1953): ‘According to some early maps, the Yuchi had a town in this State on a river which appears to be identical with Green River.’ Which maps, and their dates, are not given, and no Kentucky town, date or county is documented, so nothing is drawn in Kentucky. Low–medium confidence.
overlapNote: Cherokee (who destroyed Chestowee in 1714), Creek (Coweta and the lower towns on the Chattahoochee), Shawnee on the Savannah River, and the Chisca, a distinct people according to Worth. Overlap with the Cherokee and Shawnee tints is expected.
basis: Spanish and English colonial records, archaeology and Swanton’s handbook, read through Wikipedia, the Tennessee Encyclopedia, the Jackson volume and Access Genealogy. Mostly tertiary web sources.

eras.label: 1567–1714 · Tennessee River valley
eras.text: The Yuchi appear as ‘Uchi’ and ‘Huchi’ in the Juan Pardo expedition of 1567, separate from the Chisca (Worth, in the Jackson volume). Sources put Yuchi bands on the Tennessee River in the 1600s and early 1700s; their last town there, Chestowee, was destroyed by the Cherokee in 1714. The sources disagree on its county: Wikipedia says Bradley County and Swanton, through Access Genealogy, says Polk County, so the tint covers both. 1567 is the year of the first naming, not of a town; the tint shows only the last town, a general area, because the Tennessee Encyclopedia notes frequent changes of location.
eras.apprTag: Approximate general area · the sources disagree on the county

eras.label: 1715–c.1721 · Chattahoochee River
eras.text: After the destruction of Chestowee in 1714 the Tennessee Encyclopedia says the Savannah River band relocated to the Chattahoochee River around 1715 and became part of the Creek Confederacy. A chapter in the Jackson volume covers the Yuchi on the Chattahoochee and Flint rivers from 1715 to 1836. The tint is Russell County, Alabama, where Euchee Town stood near Coweta Old Town: a general area. Some Yuchi stayed scattered in Tennessee; that is not drawn.

eras.label: c.1722–1751 · Savannah River and Chattahoochee
eras.text: Mount Pleasant, on the Savannah River in Effingham County, Georgia, is noted from about 1722 to about 1750, with a British trading post and small garrison; a Yuchi town at Silver Bluff, Aiken County, South Carolina, is dated 1746 to 1751 (Wikipedia). Swanton places Mount Pleasant ‘probably’ in Screven County, and Brier Creek, the Oconee River and the Flint River towns are text only. Euchee Town on the Chattahoochee continued. Both tints are general areas.

eras.label: 1752–1836 · Chattahoochee River until removal
eras.text: Euchee Town on the Chattahoochee was documented from the middle to late 1700s; William Bartram visited in 1778 and ranked it the largest and most compact Indian town he had seen (Wikipedia). The Jackson volume dates Yuchi Town on the Chattahoochee 1715–1836. In the 1830s the Yuchi were removed to Indian Territory (Oklahoma), which is text only and not drawn. The tint is Russell County, Alabama: a general area.

properties.note: Bradley and Polk counties, Tennessee, as whole counties: the last Yuchi town in Tennessee, Chestowee or Tsistu’yi, destroyed by the Cherokee in 1714. Wikipedia puts it in Bradley County; Swanton (via Access Genealogy) puts Tsistu’yi in Polk County, so both are tinted. Counties are used only to give a generous general area; the edge follows county lines and is not a boundary.

Effingham County, Georgia (Mount Pleasant on the Savannah River) and Aiken County, South Carolina (Silver Bluff), as whole counties. Counties are used only to give a generous general area; the edge follows county lines and is not a boundary.

Russell County, Alabama, as a whole county: Euchee Town on the Chattahoochee River, near the Fort Benning area. Counties are used only to give a generous general area; the edge follows county lines and is not a boundary.
Main-map extent: general areas (whole-county shapes, approximate), solid lines in Kentucky and sourced points.
